title: The landscape · The environment
description: Compare agentic setups by the work they support, the evidence they expose and the control they retain. Define an environment contract covering identity, tools, state, permissions, network and verification.

sections.title: The same model can mean different work for you

blocks.body:
You have a retry bug, a failing test and a clear acceptance condition. Two retries should allow the initial call and two further attempts. Chapter six gave us a way to check the repair. Now we need somewhere to do the work.

In an editor, you might keep the assistant beside you while you inspect the loop. You can answer a question immediately or notice that it has opened a generated file. In a background job, the agent must make those decisions with the brief and tools it receives. A scheduled job goes further: it also needs a standing rule for which failures deserve investigation and where the result should appear.

Each arrangement puts different work on the person using it. A chat interface may be enough to explain a trace, even if you copy the relevant code into it yourself. If you want a reviewed patch by the morning, manually transferring every command and result defeats much of that purpose. Conversely, a background job that cannot ask a necessary question may spend an hour implementing the wrong interpretation.

Start by describing the handoff you want. What will you give the system, what should come back, and what decisions will you still make along the way? That description turns a product comparison into a smaller question: which setup can support this particular collaboration?

The model, harness and workflow remain useful distinctions. The model interprets the evidence and proposes actions. The harness makes tools and observations available. The workflow determines when work starts and how it reaches review. A product may package all three, so a better result does not automatically tell us which part made the difference.

sections.title: Watch a task travel through both setups
sections.navLabel: A comparison that teaches you something

blocks.body:
**Worked Example**

Suppose a team is comparing its usual chat assistant with a repository-connected worker. The task is the retry repair from the preceding chapters. Both start from the same source revision and receive the same behavioural brief. The chat assistant relies on an engineer to supply files and run commands; the worker can search, edit and test within its checkout.

The chat produces a plausible fix quickly. The engineer then finds the relevant test command, applies the suggestion and brings the failure back into the conversation. The worker spends longer finding the implementation, but returns a diff and the command it ran. Which has saved work is still open. The chat's early answer may have hidden several minutes of human effort; the worker's report may take longer to untangle.

Follow both results to the same acceptance point. Record the engineer's interventions as well as elapsed time, and inspect the delivered changes using the same relevant checks. A system that needs help is not disqualified. That help is part of the operating arrangement being compared.

Now interrupt the worker after it has edited the file. Can you identify the changes it left behind? On resume, does it inspect the workspace before relying on an earlier passing test? This exposes a capability that a polished demonstration can easily hide: how much work you inherit when a run ends somewhere inconvenient.

If one setup cannot run the tests because a service is missing, name that limitation. It is a real limitation of the proposed setup, but it is not evidence that its model cannot reason about the bug. You might repair the environment and repeat the trial, or decide that the repair costs too much for this use.

Keep those two conclusions separate. An end-to-end trial can tell you which arrangement currently helps your team. Establishing why one wins requires a more controlled comparison. Changing the model, its tools and its inputs together cannot isolate a model effect.

blocks.question: One setup produces an answer sooner, but the engineer spends longer transferring files, applying edits and checking it. Has the faster setup won?
blocks.answer: Only if first-answer speed was the outcome you needed. For a repair, compare the work through acceptance, including the engineer's active effort and the quality of the delivered result. The early answer alone does not settle that comparison.

sections.title: A checkout is only part of the workplace

blocks.body:
The worker's missing service deserves a closer look. Source access lets it read a test that depends on a local service; it does not make that service exist. Likewise, a shell tool can be present while every useful command fails because the runtime or dependencies are wrong.

Before investigating the application, establish that the environment can answer the question you intend to ask. Identify the checkout and any local changes. Use the repository's documented runtime, package manager and dependency setup. Find the narrow test command and the fixtures or services it needs. Check which external connections are expected, and which inputs can be supplied locally.

For the retry helper, the focused test may need only a fake clock and scripted timeout responses. If so, production access would add little to this investigation. If the task instead concerns an integration service's behaviour, a local unit test leaves that part unresolved. The environment is ready for some claims and not others; report the distinction rather than calling the whole workspace either usable or useless.

An environment contract records these conditions so a new run can establish them without guessing. Some parts can be executable: a setup check can report an unsupported runtime or a missing fixture before the agent starts editing. Other parts belong in guidance, such as which service can be simulated and which integration claim requires a separate check.

Keep the contract connected to the repository's actual setup. A long inventory copied into every prompt will become stale. A short instruction that points to maintained setup scripts, names the working directory and explains a relevant limitation is often easier to use and repair.

sections.title: Separate a reviewable change from permission to act

blocks.body:
A branch or worktree makes a patch easier to compare, review and discard. It does not confine a process. A command running there may still reach other directories, use inherited credentials or contact external services. Version-control isolation and execution permissions solve different problems.

For a local retry repair, give the worker the capabilities required to inspect and modify its assigned checkout and run the relevant checks. Publishing a release is a separate operation with a different reason for existing. If the worker inherits a broad token simply because it was available on the machine, its possible effects now exceed the task you meant to delegate.

Apply the boundary where actions happen: the tool executor, filesystem permissions, credential scope and network configuration. Instructions help the agent choose appropriate actions, but an instruction to stay inside the checkout does not enforce that restriction.

Also consider the code the tools execute. A test command can run repository-controlled scripts. Calling the agent 'read-only' because it cannot use an edit tool would be misleading if its shell can execute code with write access. Describe the effective capabilities of the environment, including subprocesses.

You do not need to solve every deployment problem before running a local experiment. You do need to understand what that experiment can affect. A disposable fixture with limited access is a useful place to learn; successful work there should not silently become authority over a live system.

blocks.question: An agent works on its own branch but runs with the developer's normal credentials. What does the branch protect, and what does it leave exposed?
blocks.answer: The branch separates the versioned patch for review. It does not restrict the process's filesystem, network or account permissions. Commands may still affect anything those credentials and the execution environment allow.

sections.title: Choose with the remaining work in view

blocks.body:
At the end of the trial, a useful conclusion names the work that remains with you. Perhaps the editor assistant is effective for investigations where requirements evolve during conversation, while a background worker handles well-specified local repairs with less active supervision. Those can both be good choices.

The evidence may also suggest a cheaper improvement than changing products. If both systems lose time finding the test entry point, fix the repository guidance. If both produce correct patches but confusing reports, improve the handoff you ask for. If adequate evidence reaches the model and it repeatedly misinterprets the contract, then a model comparison has a clearer purpose.

Record the conditions under which the choice made sense: the task sample, model and product configuration, environment, review effort and unresolved failures. Repeat the comparison when a meaningful condition changes. A product name alone cannot preserve that conclusion.

So far, our repair fits into a relatively short investigation. The next chapter follows work that spans several stages or sessions. The environment will still matter, but now we must also decide what progress survives an interruption and how much authority to grant at each stage.
